summary: Defines the profile of the MIME directory content type for a white-pages person object, based on the vCard electronic business card. It is the format behind many contact files that people exchange. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 6350.

eli5.summary: A vCard is a digital business card. This document says how to write one so that your phone, your email and other programs can all understand it.

subtitle: A standard format for exchanging digital business cards and contact information

tldr.problem: People and applications need to exchange contact information—names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses—in a format that anyone can understand and parse. Before vCard, there was no standardized way to store this information in a portable, structured way.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2426 defines vCard 3.0, a MIME directory profile for storing personal directory information. A vCard is a text file containing structured fields for name, address, phone numbers, email, organization, photographs, and many other details. Each field has a type name (like FN for formatted name, TEL for telephone) and optional parameters describing the field (like TYPE=work or TYPE=home).
tldr.outcome: vCard became the standard format for contact data used by email clients, contact managers, phones, and web services. RFC 2426 (vCard 3.0) was replaced by RFC 6350, which updated it for modern use.

today: RFC 2426 defined vCard 3.0 and became the standard for contact information exchange. It was superseded by RFC 6350, which updated vCard to version 4.0 and addressed modern use cases while maintaining compatibility with version 3.0.

sections.title: What Is vCard?
sections.content:
A vCard is a standardized text file that stores information about a person or organization. It is based on electronic business card concepts and uses a simple line-by-line format where each line begins with a field type name, followed by optional parameters, a colon, and the value.

RFC 2426 defines vCard 3.0, a profile of the MIME Directory format ([MIME-DIR]). This means a vCard can be embedded in email messages, web pages, and other MIME-compliant systems. A vCard must begin with BEGIN:VCARD and end with END:VCARD. It must contain at least three fields: FN (formatted name), N (structured name), and VERSION:3.0.

The profile permits non-standard extensions using the prefix X-, allowing applications to add custom fields without registering them officially. This flexibility has made vCard the de facto standard for contact exchange across email clients, smartphones, contact managers, and directory services.
sections.eli5: A vCard is a text file that tells computers someone's name, phone number, email address and other contact details. Everyone agrees on how to write the information, so your phone and your computer can both understand it.

sections.title: Field Types and Structure
sections.content:
vCard defines over 25 standard field types, grouped by purpose. Each type is specified once per vCard unless explicitly allowed to repeat.

Identification types capture the person's name and image: FN (formatted name), N (structured name with family, given, additional names, prefixes and suffixes), NICKNAME, PHOTO, and BDAY (birth date).

Delivery addressing types store location information: ADR (structured address with post office box, street, city, region, postal code and country) and LABEL (formatted mailing label). Both support the TYPE parameter to specify domestic (dom) or international (intl), postal or parcel delivery, and home or work address.

Telecommunications types include TEL (telephone number with TYPE values like home, work, cell, fax, pager) and EMAIL (email address, with TYPE to distinguish internet, X.400, or preferred addresses). MAILER specifies the email software the person uses.

Geographical types store timezone and location data: TZ (time zone offset like -05:00) and GEO (latitude and longitude as decimal degrees for global positioning).

Organizational types describe work context: TITLE (job title), ROLE (business category), ORG (organization name and units), LOGO (company logo image), and AGENT (another person or vCard acting on behalf of this person, such as an assistant).

Explanatory types provide additional metadata: CATEGORIES (application categories), NOTE (supplemental comments), PRODID (product that created the vCard), REV (revision date), SORT-STRING (text for sorting in non-English locales), SOUND (pronunciation audio), UID (unique identifier), and URL (website).

Security types restrict access: CLASS (PUBLIC, PRIVATE, or CONFIDENTIAL) and KEY (public key or authentication certificate in binary format).
sections.eli5: A vCard has many fields for different kinds of information. FN is the person's name. ADR is their address. TEL is their phone number. Each piece of information is labeled so computers know what it is.

sections.title: Values and Encoding
sections.content:
Field values can be simple text, structured (with components separated by semicolons), or lists (with values separated by commas). For example, the N (name) field is structured: N:Public;John;Quinlan;Mr.;Esq. represents the family name, given name, additional names, honorific prefix, and honorific suffix.

Fields can include parameters that modify their meaning. The most common parameter is TYPE, which specifies the context (home, work, preferred) or format (JPEG for photos, VOICE for phone numbers). The VALUE parameter overrides the default value type, allowing a field to hold a URI instead of inline data. The ENCODING parameter specifies how binary data is encoded (typically base64, indicated by ENCODING=b).

Binary data like photographs, logos, sounds, and public keys must be encoded using the base64 encoding scheme. Long lines of encoded data are folded at 75 characters to comply with email message length limits. Lines longer than 75 characters are folded using a continuation method: the line ends with a space or tab, and the next line continues the value.

Special characters in field values must be escaped: semicolons, commas, and backslashes in text values are preceded by a backslash. Line breaks use the escaped sequence \n. This allows complex values (like a vCard embedded in an AGENT field) to be represented in text form while remaining parseable.
sections.eli5: Information in a vCard is stored in text form. Numbers are written as numbers. Addresses have commas separating parts. Pictures are converted to text using a special code. This way, everything fits in a simple text file.

sections.title: Parsing and Compatibility
sections.content:
vCard uses MIME Directory features for line delimiting and folding. When parsing a vCard, any folded lines (lines that start with a space or tab as a continuation) must be unfolded first by removing the whitespace and concatenating them. When writing a vCard, lines longer than 75 characters should be folded using this same method to ensure compatibility with email systems that have line-length restrictions.

RFC 2426 defines a formal grammar using ABNF notation to specify the exact syntax. This grammar ensures that parsers can reliably read vCards written by different applications.

vCard supports type grouping: a group label prepended to a type name allows related properties to be associated together. For example, work.TEL:+1-213-555-1234 and work.EMAIL:john@work.com both belong to the work group, indicating they are all work-related contact details.

The LANGUAGE parameter allows text fields to specify their language (using ISO 639 language codes), and the CHARSET parameter specifies the character encoding of text values, enabling vCards to represent international names and addresses correctly.
sections.eli5: vCard files follow strict rules about how to write each line. This ensures that any program can read and understand vCards from any other program. Some information can be labeled as work-related or home-related to group similar fields together.
